items.title: Time & Work — the LCM (units) method
items.body:
## Core idea

- **Rate of work = 1 / (days to finish alone)**; work done = rate × time.
- **LCM shortcut:** let total work = LCM of the given days, so each rate becomes a whole number of *units/day* — no fractions.

## Combined & efficiency

- Together: time = 1/(1/a + 1/b) = **ab/(a+b)**.
- 'A is k times as efficient as B' → rate ratio **k : 1**, and time ratio **1 : k** (the faster one takes fewer days).

## Worked example

A = 18 days, B = 9 days. Total = LCM(18,9) = **18 units** → A = 1 unit/day, B = 2 units/day. B works 3 days = 6 units; remaining 12 units by A = **12 days**.

## Common traps

- Never **add days** for combined work (12 + 15 ≠ answer).
- The **simple average** of the two times overstates the joint time.
keyPoints: Rate of work = 1 / days to finish alone; work = rate × time.
LCM method: set total work = LCM of days so rates are whole units/day.
Together time = ab/(a+b) = 1/(1/a + 1/b).
'k times as efficient' means rate ratio k:1 and time ratio 1:k.
Never add the individual days for combined work.
items.mnemonic: Think 'units, not fractions' — LCM turns every rate into a clean whole number.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Fractions of Work / Efficiency and Work Comparison

items.title: Alternate-days work
items.body:
## Method

1. Convert to **units** (LCM method).
2. Add one **full cycle** (e.g. A-day + B-day) to get units per cycle.
3. Count how many whole cycles fit, then **finish the remainder** with whoever's turn is next — this last stretch may be a **fraction of a day**.

## Worked example

A = 8 days (3/day), B = 12 days (2/day); total = LCM = 24 units. One 2-day cycle = 3 + 2 = 5 units. 4 cycles (8 days) = 20 units. Day 9 (A): +3 → 23. Just 1 unit left; day 10 (B, 2/day) needs 1/2 day. **Total = 9½ days.**

## Trap

- The last person may not need a full day — check the leftover units against that day's rate.
keyPoints: Alternate work: sum one full cycle (A-day + B-day) first.
Fit whole cycles, then finish the remainder with the next person's turn.
The final stretch is often a fraction of a day — do not round it up automatically.
Who starts first matters when the work finishes mid-cycle.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Alternate Days Work

items.title: Work & wages and the man-days rule
items.body:
## Wages

- **Wages ∝ work done ∝ efficiency.** Split total pay in the ratio of the workers' rates.
- Example: A (6 days) and B (8 days) → ratio 1/6 : 1/8 = **4 : 3**; on ₹2800, A = ₹1600, B = ₹1200 (the faster worker earns more).

## Man-days / man-hours

- For the **same job**, the product **M · D · H** is constant:

$$\frac{M_1 D_1 H_1}{W_1} = \frac{M_2 D_2 H_2}{W_2}$$

- Example: 10 men × 8 h × 6 days = 8 men × 10 h × D → 480 = 80D → **D = 6 days**.

## Trap

- Don't forget the **hours term** — fewer men can be offset by longer hours.
keyPoints: Wages are shared in the ratio of work done = ratio of efficiency (1/a : 1/b).
The faster worker (smaller days) earns the larger share.
M1·D1·H1 = M2·D2·H2 for the same amount of work.
Include work amount (W) in the ratio when the job size changes.
items.mnemonic: MDH = constant — More men or Hours means fewer Days.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Work and Wages / Man-Hours Concept

items.title: Pipes & cisterns
items.body:
## Idea

Pipes and cisterns are just time-and-work with **inlets = positive** (fill) and **outlets/leaks = negative** (empty).

| Situation | Net rate (tank/hour) |
|---|---|
| Two inlets a, b | 1/a + 1/b |
| Inlet a with outlet b | 1/a − 1/b |

- Time to fill = **1 ÷ net rate**. The tank fills only if the net rate is **positive** (inlet faster than outlet).

## Worked examples

- A = 6 h, B = 4 h (both inlets): rate = 1/6 + 1/4 = 5/12 → **2.4 h**.
- Inlet 10 h, outlet 15 h: net = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30 → **30 h** to fill.
keyPoints: Inlet rate is added (+), outlet/leak rate is subtracted (−).
Fill time = 1 ÷ net rate; tank fills only if net rate is positive.
Two inlets together: time = ab/(a+b).
A leak that empties in y hours reduces the inlet's effective rate by 1/y.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Pipes and Cistern

items.title: Speed–distance–time, average speed & trains
items.body:
## Basics

- **Distance = Speed × Time.** Convert **km/h → m/s by ×5/18** (and m/s → km/h by ×18/5).
- **Average speed (equal distances)** = **2xy/(x+y)** (harmonic mean), always less than (x+y)/2.
- **Change-of-speed problems:** if a distance d is late by t₁ at v₁ and early by t₂ at v₂, then d/v₁ − d/v₂ = (t₁ + t₂) in hours.

## Relative speed

- **Same direction:** relative speed = **difference** of speeds.
- **Opposite directions:** relative speed = **sum** of speeds.

## Trains

| Crossing | Distance covered |
|---|---|
| Pole / person (point object) | length of train |
| Platform / bridge | train + platform length |
| Another train | sum of both lengths (÷ relative speed) |

Example: 150 m train at 54 km/h (=15 m/s) over a 210 m platform → 360/15 = **24 s**.
keyPoints: km/h → m/s: multiply by 5/18; m/s → km/h: multiply by 18/5.
Average speed for equal distances = 2xy/(x+y), not the plain average.
Same direction → relative speed = difference; opposite → sum.
Crossing a pole/person uses train length; a platform adds the platform length; another train adds both lengths.
Early/late: d/v1 − d/v2 = total time gap in hours.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Average Speed / Relative speed / Problem on Train

items.title: Boats & streams and races
items.body:
## Boats & streams

- Let boat speed in still water = **B**, stream = **S**.
- **Downstream = B + S** (with current); **Upstream = B − S** (against current).
- Recover the two speeds: **B = (down + up)/2**, **S = (down − up)/2**.
- Example: 30 km down in 2 h (=15 km/h) and 30 km up in 3 h (=10 km/h) → B = 12.5 km/h, S = 2.5 km/h.

## Races

- 'A beats B by **d** metres' in an **L**-metre race → in equal time A runs L while B runs (L − d), so **speed ratio = L : (L − d)**.
- 'Beats by **t** seconds' → B covers that last gap in t seconds; combine with B's speed to find distances.
- A **head-start (start of x m)** means B runs (L − x) while A runs L.
keyPoints: Downstream = B + S; Upstream = B − S.
Boat speed = (down + up)/2; stream speed = (down − up)/2.
Upstream is always the slower (smaller) effective speed.
Beaten by d m in an L m race → speed ratio L : (L − d).
A 'start of x metres' means the opponent runs only (L − x).
items.mnemonic: Down-Add, Up-Under (subtract); Boat = average of the two, Stream = half their gap.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Boat and Stream / Race

items.title: Men–women–boys equivalence
items.body:
Some problems give a **conversion between worker types** (e.g. 2 men = 3 women, or 1 man = 2 boys). The trick is to **reduce every worker to one common unit** before applying the man-days rule.

## Method

1. Use the given relation to express all workers in one type (say, women).
2. Compute total work in **worker-days**: W = (equivalent workers) × days.
3. Re-divide W by the new equivalent workforce to get the new time.

## Worked example

2 men = 3 women ⇒ 1 man = 1.5 women. So 6 men + 6 women = 9 + 6 = **15 women**. If they finish in 8 days, W = 15 × 8 = 120 woman-days; 12 women take 120 ÷ 12 = **10 days**.

## Trap

- Never add men and women directly — convert first. A man-count and a woman-count are different 'currencies' until you apply the exchange rate.
keyPoints: Convert all worker types to one common unit using the given equivalence (e.g. 2 men = 3 women).
Total work in worker-days = equivalent workers × days, and is constant.
Two teams that each finish in time t together take t/2 (rates add).
Do not add different worker types before converting them.
items.mnemonic: One currency first — convert men↔women↔boys before you count days.
